question.:question/worked-solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $49{x}^{2}=(7x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=7x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{7\sqrt{1-49{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(7x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{7}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{49}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{49}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{49}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(7x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{49-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{49\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/49)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/49}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/7)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$  

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{49-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/7)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (7\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{11})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{11}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{11}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=11\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{121-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3}{11}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/11)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{11}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (11\,\text{d}u) \\  & =3\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{11})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
